steps.title: In the ground
steps.text: Tin's ore is cassiterite, a dense brown oxide that forms in veins around granite. Rivers have washed much of it out and laid it down in gravels, along a belt from Myanmar through Thailand and Malaysia to the Indonesian islands, and off their coasts.

shares.caption: World reserves, of the quantified total

steps.india: Token quantities from small placer deposits.

steps.title: Mine
steps.text: Gravel deposits are worked with dredges and water jets, on land and on the sea bed, often by small operators. Hard-rock veins in China, Peru and Bolivia are mined underground.

steps.title: Concentrate
steps.text: Cassiterite is about seven times as dense as water, so it is separated by gravity: jigs and shaking tables wash the lighter sand away.

steps.title: Smelt and refine
steps.text: The concentrate is melted with carbon in a furnace, which strips the oxygen and leaves crude tin. Tin melts at 232°C, so it is refined by melting it gently off its impurities, and by electrolysis for the purest grades.
steps.india: Domestic output, mostly from recycling, meets 10 to 20% of consumption.

steps.title: Make
steps.text: Tin is alloyed into solder wire and paste, plated onto steel sheet to make tinplate, and reacted into organic tin chemicals. It is cast with copper into bronze.

steps.title: Use
steps.text: Solder holds every circuit board together and is tin's largest use worldwide. Tinplate makes food cans, tin chemicals stabilise PVC, and tin is alloyed into the lead grids of batteries.
steps.india: Electronics, tinplate and chemical makers; more than 80% is imported.

steps.title: Recycle
steps.text: Solder dross and factory scrap are remelted, tin is stripped from tinplate scrap, and it returns in recycled bronze and lead alloys. Recycled metal is a large part of supply.
